Content:
Consider a population in which an unknown proportion [MATH: p] of individuals has a particular characteristic. Suppose we draw an independent random sample of size [MATH: n] from this population and use it to find an estimate for [MATH: p.]

Content:
By the central limit theorem, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] can be approximated as
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\right).]
For this approximation to be valid, we require that

Content:
- more than five sample elements have the characteristic [MATH: (np>5),] and
- more than five sample elements do not have the characteristic [MATH: (n(1-p)>5).]

Content:
This approximation assumes that the population from which the sample is drawn is infinite. So what happens when the population is finite?

Content:
Similar to previous cases we've seen, we can apply a finite population correction factor whenever a sample is conducted without replacement, and the population size is not large compared to the sample size. In such cases, the distribution of the sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} \right),]
where [MATH: N] is the population size.

Content:
The correction factor should be applied whenever the sample size is at least [MATH: 5\%] of the population size.
[MATH: n > 5\%\cdot N]

Content:
Finally, note that if samples are drawn with replacement, each element can be selected multiple times. This effectively makes the population infinite, so the correction factor is unnecessary in this case.

Given a population of [MATH: N] individuals in which a proportion [MATH: p] of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] can be approximated as

[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} \right),]

where

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size,

  • [MATH: np > 5] (more than [MATH: 5] sample elements have the characteristic), and

  • [MATH: n(1-p) > 5] (more than [MATH: 5] sample elements do not have the characteristic).

The factor [MATH: \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}] is the finite population correction factor for the variance. This is used in cases of finite samples where

  • [MATH: n\gt 5\%\cdot N] (i.e., the sample comprises more than [MATH: 5\%] of the population), and

  • the sample is conducted without replacement.

If a sample is conducted from a finite population with replacement, then the sample data are independent, and a finite population correction factor is not required.

In our case, we have [MATH: N = 480 + 320 = 800, \qquad p=\dfrac{320}{800} = 0.4, \qquad 5\%\cdot N = 40.]

Let's now examine each situation. In all cases, we are told that [MATH: np>5, n(1-p)>5.] So, we only need to check the requirement [MATH: n\gt 5\%\cdot N] and that the samples are conducted without replacement.

  • In situation I, we have [MATH: n \leq 40.] Since the sample size is smaller than [MATH: 5\%] of the population, the finite population correction factor is not necessary when modeling the distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}.]

  • In situation II, since the sample is conducted with replacement, the finite population correction factor is not necessary when modeling the distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}.]

  • In situation III, we have [MATH: n \gt 40.] Since the sample size is larger than [MATH: 5\%] of the population and the sample is conducted without replacement, the finite population correction factor is necessary when modeling the distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

sections.normalized_html:
Given a population of [MATH: N] individuals in which a proportion [MATH: p] of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] can be approximated as

[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} \right),]

where

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size,

  • [MATH: np > 5] (more than [MATH: 5] sample elements have the characteristic), and

  • [MATH: n(1-p) > 5] (more than [MATH: 5] sample elements do not have the characteristic).

The factor [MATH: \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}] is the finite population correction factor for the variance. This is used in cases of finite samples where

  • [MATH: n\gt 5\%\cdot N] (i.e., the sample comprises more than [MATH: 5\%] of the population), and

  • The sample is conducted without replacement.

If a sample is conducted from a finite population with replacement, then the sample data are independent, and a finite population correction factor is not required.

In our case, we have [MATH: n = 30, \qquad p = 0.25, \qquad N = 100.]

Now, since [MATH: n|> 5% ⋅ 100 = 5; np|= 30(0.25) = 7.5 > 5; n(1 − p)|= 30(0.75) = 22.5 > 5] we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

[MATH: p^(^)|∼N(p, (p(1 − p))/(n) ⋅ (N − n)/(N − 1)); ∼N(0.25, (0.25(1 − 0.25))/(30) ⋅ (70)/(99)); ∼N(0.25, (7)/(1584)).]

The probability we wish to find is [MATH: P\left(0.35 \lt \widehat{\,p} \lt 0.5\right).] So, we convert [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] to a standard normal random variable by [MATH: z]-scoring:

[MATH: P(0.35 < p^(^) < 0.5)|= P((0.35 − 0.25)/(sqrt((7)/(1584))) < Z < (0.5 − 0.25)/(sqrt((7)/(1584)))); ≈ P(1.50 < Z < 3.76); = P(Z < 3.76) − P(Z < 1.50); = Φ(3.76) − Φ(1.50)]

Therefore, [MATH: P\left(0.35 \lt \widehat{\,p} \lt 0.5\right) \approx \Phi(3.76) - \Phi(1.50).]

Given a population of [MATH: N] individuals in which a proportion [MATH: p] of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] can be approximated as

[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} \right),]

where

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size,

  • [MATH: np > 5] (more than [MATH: 5] sample elements have the characteristic), and

  • [MATH: n(1-p) > 5] (more than [MATH: 5] sample elements do not have the characteristic).

The factor [MATH: \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}] is the finite population correction factor for the variance. This is used in cases of finite samples where

  • [MATH: n\gt 5\%\cdot N] (i.e., the sample comprises more than [MATH: 5\%] of the population), and

  • the sample is conducted without replacement.

If a sample is conducted from a finite population with replacement, then the sample data are independent, and a finite population correction factor is not required.

In our case, we have [MATH: n = 32, \qquad p = 0.8, \qquad N = 182.]

Now, since [MATH: n|> 5% ⋅ 182 = 9.1; np|= 32(0.8) = 25.6 > 5; n(1 − p)|= 32(0.2) = 6.4 > 5] we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

[MATH: p^(^)|∼N(p, (p(1 − p))/(n) ⋅ (N − n)/(N − 1)); ∼N(0.8, (0.8(1 − 0.8))/(32) ⋅ (150)/(181)); ∼N(0.8, (3)/(724)).]

The probability we wish to find is [MATH: P\left( \widehat{\,p} \geq \dfrac{24}{32}\right) = P\left( \widehat{\,p} \geq 0.75 \right).] So, we convert [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] to a standard normal random variable by [MATH: z]-scoring:

[MATH: P(p^(^) ≥ 0.75)|= P(Z ≥ (0.75 − 0.8)/(sqrt((3)/(724)))); = P(Z ≥ − 0.78); = 1 − P(Z < − 0.78); = 1 − Φ(− 0.78)]

From the table, we have [MATH: Φ(− 0.78) = 0.2177.]

Therefore, [MATH: P(p^(^) ≥ 0.75)|= 1 − Φ(− 0.78); = 1 − 0.2177; = 0.7823.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider a population in which an unknown proportion [MATH: p] of individuals has a particular characteristic. Suppose we draw an independent random sample of size [MATH: n] from this population and use it to find an estimate for [MATH: p.]

Content:
By the central limit theorem, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] can be approximated as
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\right).]
For this approximation to be valid, we require that

Content:
- more than five sample elements have the characteristic [MATH: (np>5),] and
- more than five sample elements do not have the characteristic [MATH: (n(1-p)>5).]

Content:
This approximation assumes that the population from which the sample is drawn is infinite. So what happens when the population is finite?

Content:
Similar to previous cases we've seen, we can apply a finite population correction factor whenever a sample is conducted without replacement, and the population size is not large compared to the sample size. In such cases, the distribution of the sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} \right),]
where [MATH: N] is the population size.

Content:
The correction factor should be applied whenever the sample size is at least [MATH: 5\%] of the population size.
[MATH: n > 5\%\cdot N]

Content:
Finally, note that if samples are drawn with replacement, each element can be selected multiple times. This effectively makes the population infinite, so the correction factor is unnecessary in this case.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Situations Where a Correction Factor Is Necessary

Example Prompt:
A container contains [MATH: 480] yellow peppers and [MATH: 320] red peppers. We wish to construct a statistical model for [MATH: \widehat{\,p},] the proportion of red peppers in a random sample.

Consider the following random samples.

1. [MATH: 35] peppers are drawn from the container without replacement.
2. [MATH: 40] peppers are drawn from the container with replacement.
3. [MATH: 50] peppers are drawn from the container without replacement.

Which of these sampling methods requires a finite population correction factor to be applied to model [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] as normal?

Hint: In all cases, the requirement [MATH: np>5] and [MATH: n(1-p)>5] is satisfied.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Given a population of [MATH: N] individuals in which a proportion [MATH: p] of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] can be approximated as

[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} \right),]

where

- [MATH: n] is the sample size,
- [MATH: np > 5] (more than [MATH: 5] sample elements have the characteristic), and
- [MATH: n(1-p) > 5] (more than [MATH: 5] sample elements do not have the characteristic).

The factor
[MATH: \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}]
is the finite population correction factor for the variance. This is used in cases of finite samples where

- [MATH: n\gt 5\%\cdot N] (i.e., the sample comprises more than [MATH: 5\%] of the population), and
- the sample is conducted without replacement.

If a sample is conducted from a finite population with replacement, then the sample data are independent, and a finite population correction factor is not required.

In our case, we have
[MATH: N = 480 + 320 = 800, \qquad p=\dfrac{320}{800} = 0.4, \qquad 5\%\cdot N = 40.]

Let's now examine each situation. In all cases, we are told that [MATH: np>5, n(1-p)>5.] So, we only need to check the requirement [MATH: n\gt 5\%\cdot N] and that the samples are conducted without replacement.

- In situation I, we have [MATH: n \leq 40.] Since the sample size is smaller than [MATH: 5\%] of the population, the finite population correction factor is not necessary when modeling the distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}.]
- In situation II, since the sample is conducted with replacement, the finite population correction factor is not necessary when modeling the distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}.]
- In situation III, we have [MATH: n \gt 40.] Since the sample size is larger than [MATH: 5\%] of the population and the sample is conducted without replacement, the finite population correction factor is necessary when modeling the distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".
